chapters.summary: Staff welcomes attendees to the Government Operations hearing, asks everyone to silence devices, bans food and drink, and says no one may approach the dais. Staff also directs anyone submitting in-person testimony to the sergeant at arms.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and sets room rules

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's hearing for government operations, state and federal.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please everyone silence all and any electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Also, there is no eating food or beverages here in the hearing room.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Also, at this point, moving forward, no one, I repeat, no one is to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Finally, if you wish to submit an in-person testimony, please see one of the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair and speaker, we're ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Brewer identifies herself as chair of the Committee on Government Operations, State and Federal Legislation and thanks attendees. She notes Council Member Morano's presence and turns to Speaker Menin for opening remarks.
chapters.title: Chair Brewer opens hearing on ethnic and community media oversight

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm Gail Brewer, Chair of Committee on Government Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to thank everyone for joining us today for our hearing on the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Members of the public and everyone who joins us today, I think I see Councilmember Morano.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know where he went, but he was here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll now turn it over to Speaker Menon for her opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Brewer and recalls starting city investment in ethnic and community media over a decade ago. She describes a 2016 million-dollar CUNY journalism grant and reads her earlier statement that ethnic media reflects New York's diversity.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin recounts early city investment in ethnic media

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Brewer, and I really want to thank the chair for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm Julie Menon, speaker of the New York City Council, and we want to thank members of the public for being here today for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So this issue that we are discussing today around the mayor's office of community and

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: ethnic media is not new to the city council and it's certainly not a new issue for me.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I've long recognized the importance of ethnic and community media, which led me to start investing in that over a decade ago.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In 2016, when I served as commissioner of the mayor's office of media and entertainment,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We announced a million-dollar grant to CUNY's journalism school to create new programs that would help New York City's community and ethnic media outlets stay competitive and bring them further into the digital age.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we were really proud to announce that program.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: At that announcement, here is what I said.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The diversity and breadth of New York City's community and ethnic media reflects the diversity of our city as a whole, and it is crucially important to keep these outlets thriving.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These publications add key perspective to our local news landscape, and they keep New Yorkers in the know, whether their native language is English or Bangla.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We look forward to collaborating with the Journalism School on this important initiative, which builds on their history of providing excellent training for journalists at ethnic and community publications.

chapters.summary: Menin explains that Local Law 83 codified Executive Order 47 and requires mayoral agencies to spend at least 50% of advertising budgets with ethnic and community media. She says spending peaked at $23.1 million in 2022 but overall city ad spending fell sharply, leaving only $7 million for ethnic media in 2024.
chapters.title: Menin details Local Law 83 mandate and declining ad dollars

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that quote that I mentioned almost a decade ago still rings incredibly true today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is why the council passed Local Law 83 in 2021 to formally establish the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: community media, codifying former Mayor de Blasio's Executive Order 47.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Local Law 83 also requires mayoral agencies to spend at least 50% of their advertising budget on ethnic and community media outlets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The Council passed this bill because we recognize the crucial role that community and ethnic media plays in our city and to address the difficult media climate for small publications.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I also want to add I really appreciate the incredible work that our community and ethnic media outlets provide and that is why

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: when I served as a 2020 census director we proudly allocated half of our media budget to community and ethnic outlets all across the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I do want to say that when former Mayor de Blasio made that change in policy and the council passed that law, it had a significant impact.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Prior to the implementation of Executive Order 47 and Local Law 83, 82% of the city's advertising spending went to large mainstream media outlets, whereas ethnic and community media outlets only received $2.7 million

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: in the city's advertising budget.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: By 2020, the first full year of implementation, that amount increased to $9.9 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: City spending on ethnic and community media peaked in 2022 when it reached a high of $23.1 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2025, 57% of city agencies' overall advertising spending went towards ethnic and community media.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It was 51% for fiscal year 24 and 40% for fiscal year 23.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: However, that has not translated into greater monetary benefits because overall advertising spending has decreased significantly.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2022, the city spent $260 million on advertising across all media outlets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: However, that number dropped to $70.4 million in fiscal year 2023, $28.8 million in fiscal year 2024.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In 2024, just $7 million of those dollars went to ethnic and community media, less than a third of what it was.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Two years before that.

chapters.summary: Menin says the Council held roundtables with Black, Asian, and Latino publishers between June and July. Publishers reported no city point of contact, lost connections from prior administrations, and severe financial strain worsened by reduced city ad buys.
chapters.title: Menin reports publisher concerns from summer roundtables

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So what has changed and why is the city's spending on media so much lower than it was just a few years ago?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Over the past summer, the council convened a series of forums to better understand this issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Between June and July of this year, we hosted roundtables with Black, Asian, and Latino community media outlets at City Hall, bringing together journalists and publishers, and I know many of you came to that and we really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In these meetings, we heard firsthand concerns about the city's drastically decreased media spending and investments in ethnic and community media.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Furthermore, participants...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: expressed concerns about not having a point of contact within the city, and they felt that they didn't know how to contact the administration and that lines of connections that they had during previous administrations are now not existent.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Many also conveyed that their outlets are facing unprecedented financial troubles in this very challenging media environment for local media across the country,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and significant decrease ad buys from the city have just exacerbated those difficulties.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I know many are concerned about the moving and staffing of the mayor's office of ethnic and community media, so I know I have some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I know the chair has some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we are here to get answers from the administration, to hear from members of the media, and to understand how we can support this crucial sector, which reaches all of the diverse communities in New York City with vital, culturally sensitive reporting.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We must do more to invest in our ethnic and community media.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you so much, Chair Brewer, and let me turn it back to you.

chapters.summary: Brewer says federal pandemic money and census outreach showed how vital ethnic media is for public health information. She lists the oversight topic and four bills: Intros 1127, 1128, 1129, and her preconsidered working-group bill on communication technologies.
chapters.title: Brewer links pandemic and census outreach to four bills on agenda

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I think during the pandemic, some of the federal money helped a lot.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And you could see the difference because health information got out, and then you did a great job during the census doing the same.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So we know how important that media is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In addition to oversight, we will be hearing four bills.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The first bill, Intro 1127, sponsored by Councilmember Williams.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In relation to mending and eliminating certain

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: reporting requirements within the New York City Charter and the Administrative Code of the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro number 1128, also sponsored by Councilmember Williams, in relation to due dates of agency reports to the Council.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro 1129, in relation to agency transmissions of reports.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Of compliance with operational requirements and pre-considered intro, which I sponsored in relation to the creation of a working group to study agency use of communication technologies.

chapters.summary: Brewer says Local Law 83 requires agencies to spend at least 50% of broadcast, print, and digital advertising with ethnic and community media. She notes social media and digital displays are out of scope and that agencies can receive waivers in limited cases.
chapters.title: Brewer explains Local Law 83 scope and 50% advertising requirement

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Local Law 83, like Executive Order 47 before it, 83 just codified and added to,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: requires agency to spend, as you heard earlier, at least 50% of their advertising budget with ethnic and community media outlets.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We are hearing from community and ethnic media outlets that under the current mayor, they are seeing an up to 100% drop in city advertising revenue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Since Mayor Mondami took office, we would like to find out whether this is true, and if so, why city advertising with these outlets has decreased so drastically between one administration and the other.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Local Law 83 of 2021, requirement that agencies...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Spend at least 50% of their budget, their advertising budget, on ethnic and community media doesn't apply to the agency's entire spending budget.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But to spend...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: spending on broadcast, print, and digital advertising.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Other types of advertising, such as social media and digital displays, are considered out of scope and not subject to the 50% spending requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They might not have existed in 2021.

chapters.summary: Brewer explains waivers for legal mandates or agencies spending under $5,000 annually, and says many agencies fall into that category. She says the office must report annually on agency spending and maintain a directory that currently lists about 293 outlets.
chapters.title: Brewer details waivers, annual report, and 293-outlet directory

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Agencies can also be granted waivers

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: if they were required by statute, court order, or legal mandate to publish information in media outlets that reach all New Yorkers, or

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: if, as an agency, they spend less than $5,000 per year on advertising.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And there's quite a long list that spend less than $5,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Local Law 83 also created the Office of Ethnic and Community Media, which is tasked with submitting an annual report

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: on agency spending on ethnic and community media, as well as developing and maintaining a directory of community and ethnic media outlets for agencies to use when complying with Local Law 83's spending mandate.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And looking at the most recent 2-5 report, it looks like there's about 293 such media outlets.

chapters.summary: Brewer says the mayor first moved the Office of Ethnic and Community Media into Mass Engagement, then later into the communications office. She says the executive director left at the end of 2025 and no replacement was appointed until September 2026.
chapters.title: Brewer describes MOECM moves and eight-month leadership gap

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: On one of his first days in office, the mayor moved the Office of Ethnic and Community Media into the Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Ethnic and community media outlets welcomed the move.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They viewed it as a signal that that media was being valued as both channels

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: for messaging but also as partners in helping New Yorkers understand and participate in civic

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: However, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The executive director left at the end of 2-5, and no new executive director was appointed until September of this year, after the office was moved again, this time into the mayor's director of communications office.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: When asked about OCM,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: At a previous hearing, the Commissioner of the Office of Mass Engagement was unable to answer the questions about the office, despite it being part of mass engagement for a year.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Commissioner referred questions to the Director of Communications.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We hope the new Executive Director, thank you for being here today, will be able to address the many concerns we are hearing from community and ethnic media outlets.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As well as the questions we have about the function of the office, including the website.

chapters.summary: Brewer says a prior hearing revealed a Signal group used by the mayor with auto-delete enabled and that the records commissioner called instant messages transitory. Her preconsidered bill would create a working group to study agency use of messaging platforms and recommend retention rules.
chapters.title: Brewer introduces working-group bill on agency messaging technologies

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In addition to oversight of the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media and government spending on ads, we will be hearing my bill, pre-considered intro, which would create, as you heard earlier, a group to study agency use.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Of communication technologies.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: At our hearing last month, we heard about a signal group used by the mayor to communicate with social media influencers and how for a period of time, the messengers were set to auto-delete, which upsets me because I'm a big foil addict.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: At the same hearing, the Commissioner of Doris explained that instant messages are considered transitory, and therefore there is no requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that they be archived.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: While there are legitimate uses for city employees to use encrypted messaging apps like Signal, it is incredibly important that we keep records of all official communications.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This bill would require Doris to establish a working group to

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: study the instant electronic messaging platforms used by the city agencies and submit recommendations.

chapters.summary: Brewer says the Council should periodically review reporting mandates to ensure data is timely, relevant, and not duplicative. She describes Intros 1127, 1128, and 1129 as good-government bills and thanks committee and personal staff.
chapters.title: Brewer frames reporting-review bills as good government

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I also want to highlight the three good government bills we are hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It is important to the city to reevaluate the local laws that it passes, especially those that require city agencies to collect and report out data.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Reviewing and making sure that the information we receive is timely, relevant, and worth the burden is an exercise in good government.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And where we can repeal unnecessary duplicative or outdated reporting requirements, it makes it all the more worth it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: With that in mind, we are hearing intro 1127, as I said earlier, sponsored by Councilmember Williams, who will make a statement in a minute,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and then amends and eliminates certain reporting requirements within the city charter and the admin code.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro 1128, sponsored by Williams, amends the due dates of agency reports to the council.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 1129 amends agency transmissions of reports of compliance with operational requirements.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to thank the following council staff for their work.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: work on this hearing from government ops committee staff, Johari Frazier, Erica Cohen, and Sigmil Humad, and from my staff, Shuler Puder and Cynthia Horning.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think we'll now hear from Councilmember Wynn, but I also want to mention Councilmembers Wang, and I did mention Councilmember Moran earlier, but he had gone to get some coffee at the time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We'd love to hear from you, Councilmember Williams.

chapters.summary: Williams thanks Menin and Brewer and says government cannot be accountable if residents do not know what it is doing. She says the Council needs data to make policy and periodically reviews charter and code reporting burdens.
chapters.title: Williams says transparency and data access drive good-government package

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I would like to thank Speaker Menon and Chair Brewer for being here today and convening this hearing on the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media and Government Spending on Advertisements.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Government cannot be responsible to the people if the people do not know what the government is doing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Ensuring that our messaging is reaching people where they are at is critical for governmental transparency and accountability, and this is what good governing is.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Part of good governing is also ensuring that we, as the legislative branch of government, have access to the data and information we need in order to be an effective policymaking body.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: There are many obligations that our local laws place on the mayoral administration and city agencies, and we are here at the city council are very mindful of that burden.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As part of our due diligence as a steward of good governing, we periodically review the charter and administrative code to reduce unnecessary burdens on city agency staff and repeal or streamline outdated reporting or other duplicative or unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: requirements.

chapters.summary: Williams says Intro 1127 would repeal or amend 25 reporting and study provisions, Intro 1128 would create uniform default report due dates, and Intro 1129 would establish an attestation procedure for operational mandates. She thanks committee staff and her team, including Malcolm.
chapters.title: Williams outlines Intros 1127, 1128, and 1129

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Having engaged with city agencies, I am proud to be the sponsor of the Good Government Bill Package being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Proposed Introduction 1127B will repeal or amend 25 provisions of the Charter and Administrative Code requiring certain reports and studies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Introduction 1128 will create a uniform default reporting due date system for agency reports.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And Introduction 1129 will establish a procedure to be proscribed by the Speaker for how an agency will attest to the Council that it has completed operational mandates proscribed by local laws.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Taken together, these bills have us working smarter and more effectively.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They will bring efficiencies to the work this city does, and I am thankful to the chair for hearing them here today.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank the committee staff for preparing for today's hearing and to my own team for the hard work they do day in and day out.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I love how the compliance division.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Who helped me create these talking points, didn't add a line to thank them for their hard work.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So thank you, Malcolm, for your hard work in helping to draft these bills and ensuring that the council, again, is a responsive and responsible steward of city government and making sure that we reduce unnecessary things.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks Williams and says the committee counsel will swear in the administration witness. Counsel administers the affirmation, and Mazen Sidahmed answers that he will tell the truth.
chapters.title: Committee swears in administration witness

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And now we'll swear you in with the wonderful counsel to this committee.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you for already raising your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Sidahmed introduces himself as the newly appointed executive director of the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media. He says New York City cannot work for everyone if residents cannot access information and describes a national decline in local news.
chapters.title: New MOECM Executive Director Sidahmed warns of local news crisis

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Good morning, Speaker Menon and Chair Brewer and members of the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to be here with you today.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: My name is Mazen Siddahmed, and I'm the newly appointed Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'm excited to share my vision and hopes for the future of this office and Local Law 83 in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Let me start with a simple truth.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: New York City cannot work for everyone if everyone cannot access the information they need.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: This is why Local Law 83 is a truly transformative law.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Across the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And globally, local news is disappearing.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: For more than two decades, the news industry has been battered by shifting business models, changing user behavior, and growing concentration of corporate media ownership.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Since 2001, the newspaper industry has lost more jobs in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Than coal mining.

chapters.summary: Sidahmed cites Northwestern University data that a quarter of ethnic media outlets nationwide shut down since the pandemic. He says closures cost trusted information, neighborhood connections, and democratic accountability.
chapters.title: Sidahmed says community and ethnic media are hit hardest by local news decline

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Community and ethnic media have been hit the hardest.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Since the pandemic, Northwestern University's local news initiative found a quarter of ethnic media outlets nationwide shut down.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Many of these...

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: publications are small, family-owned businesses operating on the thinnest of margins.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: They serve communities that are often overlooked by larger media organizations, and they are struggling to survive.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: When a local newsroom closes, we lose more than a publication.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: We lose a source of trusted information.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: We lose a connection between neighbors and the institutions that shape their lives.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: The biggest casualty in all of this is our democracy.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Researchers link the decline of local journalism to weaker civic engagement, less accountability for public officials, and greater political polarization.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That means fewer people are asking the questions government needs to answer.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: When local stories disappear, the issues affecting our neighborhoods can disappear from public view.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: The crisis of local news has led people around the country organizing to rebuild our local news ecosystem and asking an important question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: What role can government play in sustaining local journalism?

chapters.summary: Sidahmed says Local Law 83 is a groundbreaking effort to use public resources to support local news. He explains its first pillar: ensuring every New Yorker can access public information through publications in dozens of languages.
chapters.title: Sidahmed calls Local Law 83 a national model and explains first pillar

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Local Law 83 offers an answer.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: It is a groundbreaking effort, the first attempt in the nation to put public resources to work supporting the local news outlets that help our democracy function.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: It has become a shining light for cities across the country, with many hoping to replicate this approach.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: On its face, it is a very straightforward law.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: New York City government must aim to spend 50% of its advertising budget with community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: But underlying that are two pillars that provide us with compounding benefits.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: First of all, it ensures that every New Yorker can access the critical public

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: programs and information that government provides.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: In New York City, we are blessed with publications that publish in dozens of languages.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: They are trusted messengers in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Through them, we can ensure that nobody is left behind on any government initiative that is intended to support everyone in the city.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: As immigrants across New York City are under attack, this could not be more important.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Access to accurate, timely information can make the difference between a family receiving the support it is entitled to and a family being left behind.

chapters.summary: Sidahmed says the second pillar is sustaining journalists and publications that hold institutions accountable. He lists his core duties: train agencies on Local Law 83, manage the citywide marketing directory, and publish an annual report on progress toward the 50% goal.
chapters.title: Sidahmed explains second pillar and MOECM's core duties

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: The second pillar is sustaining the journalists and publications that keep our communities informed and our institutions accountable.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: These publications are key to our civic infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: We need them to attend local community board hearings, ask their local electeds tough questions, and critically, uplift the issues that are most pressing for their communities.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Local Law 83 recognizes that supporting these outlets and connecting New Yorkers with public information are not competing goals.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: They reinforce one another.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: When community media is stronger, New Yorkers are better informed.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And when New Yorkers are better informed, our democracy is stronger.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That leads us to the creation and role of this office.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: It is the first and only of its kind nationwide.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: My responsibility is to serve as an advocate for this community of publishers across New York City government and help ensure that Local Law 83 delivers on its promise to have agencies spend marketing dollars with community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: My core responsibility is to help the community.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: are to one, train all the New York City agencies on their obligations under Local Law 83 and how to comply with the law,

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: to manage the citywide marketing directory, which identifies the publications city agencies can work with to meet their obligations, and three, publish an annual report assessing the government's progress towards the law's 50% advertising spending goal.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: These responsibilities may sound administrative, but their consequences are real.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: The way we implement this law determines whether public dollars reach the outlets that need them, whether agencies effectively communicate with New Yorkers, and whether the city delivers on the commitments it has made.

chapters.summary: Sidahmed says he started earlier this month and has already heard from many publishers. He is gathering data from media buyers and agencies to compile the FY26 Local Law 83 report and understand where spending stands.
chapters.title: Sidahmed says he is gathering FY26 data and meeting publishers

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I started in this role earlier this month.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: In this short time, I've already heard from many publishers.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I hope to spend the first few months of my role hearing their concerns, as well as any concerns internally from government agencies about the obstacles they encounter in meeting their obligations.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I am also gathering data from the city's media buyers and the agencies to compile the FY26 report on Local Law 83.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That report will help us better understand where the city stands, where progress has been made, and where we need to do more.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I am approaching this work with a clear-eyed understanding of the challenges and a recognition of what this law has already made possible.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Throughout the country, attempts to replicate this law have struggled to move from legislative ambition to effective implementation.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: New York City has spent five years building the infrastructure to make this law work, directing millions of dollars in advertising.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: to community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Those are real results.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Without that investment, who knows how many community institutions that help New Yorkers stay informed might no longer exist.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I am grateful to the people who built this office before me and to you, the City Council, for your continued interest in this office and this law.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: This sustained engagement is necessary if we are to ensure that Local Law 83 succeeds.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'm incredibly excited about what the future holds for community and ethnic media here in New York and what role this office can play in ensuring that it continues to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'd be pleased to answer your questions.

chapters.summary: Menin asks for the office's current budget and staff size. Sidahmed says he is currently the only person on the team and plans to hire after assessing publisher and agency needs; Menin says she finds that hard to believe given the office's mandate.
chapters.title: Menin questions MOECM budget and staffing; Sidahmed says he is alone

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So my first question is, what is the current size of your budget, and how many staff members do you have?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So currently you're looking at the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'm the only person on the team, but I'm really excited to be bringing on somebody in the near future.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And I think what we want to do with this office moving forward is really understand what the needs of the publishers are,

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: listen to the publishers, listen to the agencies, understand how they have worked with this office in the past, and then build a team that can really reflect those needs and how we want to move forward as an office.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I just find that hard to believe you're the only person in this office, and yet you have an enormous responsibility to ensure that 50% of the mayoral agencies,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: ad buys goes to community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I appreciate the question and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I do think that, as I mentioned, listening to the publishers and listening to the agencies is going to be really critical in these first months to understand how we can ensure this law is successful moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think you highlighted some of the concerns of the past, and I've been hearing from publishers about some of their concerns.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I'm excited to spend some time really trying to understand how we can build a team that can really ensure that this office is successful in the future.

chapters.summary: Menin asks for the total mayoral agency advertising budget so the 50% target can be measured. Sidahmed says he is collecting media-buyer reports and agency data for the FY26 report; Menin calls it a basic number and urges him to deliver it quickly.
chapters.title: Menin presses Sidahmed for overall mayoral ad budget

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, just to be clear, the law was incredibly successful.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's now been gutted.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that is why we're having this hearing, because we're deeply concerned about what is happening now.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What is the overall current advertising budget of the mayoral city agency?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So when we're talking about 50% going to the community and ethnic, what is that overall amount?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I've been hired actually to do that report and try and understand that exact thing.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So in my first few weeks in the job, I've been reaching out to the different media buyers to get reports from each of them on where they placed.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Ads over the past FY26.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I need to collect all of those reports and then take them back to each individual agency to understand if those line up with their internal data.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And then I should

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: be able to publish all of that information in the FY26 report?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I just think this is honestly concerning that we don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, that is a very basic number.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I say this as someone who is commissioner of several agencies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's that each agency has their advertising budget, and it's a very straightforward number.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So this should not take a long time to do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We would urge you to get that number to the council, to this committee, as soon as possible, because this should be very, very basic what that number is.

chapters.summary: Menin asks why the office was moved under Mass Engagement and then under the mayor's communications director, and why it had no director for eight months. Sidahmed says he cannot speak to deliberations before he joined.
chapters.title: Menin challenges office moves and eight months without a director

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Why was the Office of Ethnic and Community Media moved originally under the Office of Mass Engagement?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thanks for the question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I can't speak to the liberations that were happening prior to my joining.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah, I joined earlier this month and is currently in the Director of Communications.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you answer then why it remained under the Office of Mass Engagement for eight months and then only to be moved again and then placed under the Mayor's Director of Communications?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't really speak to deliberations that happened before I started.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, and you can't comment on why the office didn't have a director for eight months.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, that is very concerning as well, that no one was running this office.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So while it was under mass engagement for eight months and no one was running it, then it was moved again and again with no director until you came on board.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah, as I said, I can't really speak to deliberations that happened before I started, but I can say that it is a unique office.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Like I said, it's the only one of its kind in the nation.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And in my conversations in joining the administration, I did sense a real desire to really get it right and understand what would be needed for this office.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That's the only thing I can speak to.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I do just have to say, like, not having a director for eight months, moving it, originally making the decision to put it under the Office of Mass Engagement, this all begs the question of, you know, how seriously this office is really being taken.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I am someone who's worked with that office for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I really believe in community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm very troubled by what has happened over the last eight months.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And just that you can't answer the rudimentary question of, like, what is the agency's ad buy?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Like, that is a basic question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To me, like, that is, like, question number one.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What's the overall ad buy?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So then how can we make sure that 50% of it is actually going to these outlets, which is what our law prescribes?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: No, I appreciate your concern.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: As I said, I'm really looking forward to digging into the data and getting all of that information for you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'll pass it back over to Chair Brewer.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what Sidahmed's vision is for the office and notes the website is outdated. Sidahmed says he wants agencies to see community media as central to their missions and wants publisher input before making changes.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Sidahmed for his vision and a website update

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Council Member Wilson has also joined us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My other question is, what's your vision for the office?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, even the website, as you probably know, is outdated.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was looking at it this morning.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's sometimes where people see vision.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So what is your vision for the office, and when do you update?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The website.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you so much for that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: As I said, I really do.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: who see Local Law 83 as a transformative law, that it could be a law that has, as I mentioned, compounding benefits for New York City agencies and for the city as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I think my vision for the office is to really help the different New York City agencies work with me to understand the value of working with community media, that this isn't just something that you have to do because the law mandates it.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: This is critical for you to execute on your mission, whatever New York City agency you are, and work with the publishers to help them tell their story internally to different city agencies, help city agencies meet publishers and understand that,

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: okay, this publisher reaches the majority of this specific community that you need to reach for your program to succeed, and really help

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: lift up the importance of these community assets across New York so New Yorkers can really see their value.

chapters.summary: Brewer says the citywide marketing directory and office website cannot wait until next year because the current page is from 2024. Sidahmed says he does not want to make too many changes without speaking to publishers first.
chapters.title: Brewer demands website update before next year

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, and their website?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Update?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah, I would love to update the website.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Right now, I'm really trying to listen to the publishers, the agencies, the media buyers.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'd love to speak to people on the city council who really care about this office to help draft that vision.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And I think maybe early next year, I'd love to update it and write a more concrete vision for this office.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't mean to be rude, but you have to update the website before next year.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You have to.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it's 2024.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I read the whole thing this morning.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: You mean the citywide marketing directory?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, for your office.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah, so for the citywide marketing director,

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: industry. I don't

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Don't want to make too many changes to that in the near future without speaking to publishers first.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what Sidahmed will accomplish by January. Sidahmed promises to complete the FY26 report, meet most directory publishers, and provide a detailed breakdown of which outlets received city spending.
chapters.title: Brewer asks for specific January deliverables

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The other question I have is when you are, the timing of all this.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you're saying that by January you will have followed up with what the speaker suggested in terms of knowing the 50% of.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: X agency, but hopefully even before that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So what do you expect to actually have done by January?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What is your actual specific goals by January?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what your goal is.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So definitely by January, I hope to have completed the FY26 report,

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: have met with the majority of the publishers on the citywide marketing directory and heard from them about their concerns about the office and what they'd like to see the office do moving forward,

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: and have a detailed breakdown also of which outlets the government has been spending with in the last fiscal year and the fiscal years prior, because I know that's been a big source of concern for publishers too.

chapters.summary: Brewer says some directory outlets were dropped from the mayor's press list and asks why. Sidahmed refers press-list questions to the press office and says paid media should be kept separate from coverage decisions.
chapters.title: Brewer asks why outlets were removed from mayor's press list

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We also heard that some of the media outlets that are on the list currently have gotten off the mayor's press list.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you know if that's true, and if so, do you?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Can you explain why they've been taken off the mayor's press list?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because you're in that agency now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're in the communications agency.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'd encourage you to direct questions about the press list to the press office specifically.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I do think it's really important for us as we're thinking about the future of the mayor's office of ethnic and community media to separate press coverage from paid media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Because I know that some folks in the past have thought that the two things were connected and it created a sense that your press coverage may be influenced what kind of paid media you receive.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I don't want to create that impression at all.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I'd really like to focus specifically on paid media.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That comes up when the mayor had his early on influencer only press briefing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then, of course, it was quite startling that some of the ethnic and community medias were not invited.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you're saying that that's not what your job is, that that's a completely different aspect of the office that you're under.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer cites reports of up to 100% drops in city advertising and asks how fast Sidahmed can reverse it. Sidahmed says he first needs data on total spending and reallocation before making a plan.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how quickly city ad spending can recover

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We also are very concerned about the drop in city advertising.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The speaker and I also heard 100% drop in city advertising through these agencies, and that's really a huge number.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how quickly can you get them back on track?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you think you can't do that until January, or is there something you can do sooner?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because the end of 26 is very soon.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah, I think for me it's really important to understand what's going on currently.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I'm really looking forward to digging into the data and getting a deep understanding of how much money is being spent, where that money is going.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Is it a question of reallocating funds?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Is it a question of the total amount of spending?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And then making a plan based on that.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And I'll be excited to report back to you once I get that data.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what happens when agencies do not spend 50% with community media. Sidahmed says the law requires a report naming noncompliant agencies and that he will work collaboratively to increase spending.
chapters.title: Brewer asks whether agencies face penalties for missing the 50% target

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you think there are agencies that...

utterances.text: Is there some penalty for doing that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is there something we can do to make sure that they continue to do what the law calls for?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: My understanding is the law currently calls for publishing a report and explaining which agencies are not meeting their requirements.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And I've found the agencies to be really collaborative and excited to work with me.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I'm excited to work with any agency that may not be meeting its requirements, as was happening in FY25, and help them see the value of working with community media and increase that spending.

chapters.summary: Brewer notes the advertising world has changed since 2021 and asks how out-of-scope digital spending will affect traditional community media. Sidahmed says his focus is getting agencies to spend 50% with the 293 directory publications.
chapters.title: Brewer probes out-of-scope digital advertising

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you think there's any change?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Like, obviously, in today's world, there are out-of-scope advertising going on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How will you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.text: So how will the new digital opportunities or not impact the spending and impact what I consider the traditional community ethnic media?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that something that you've thought about?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think for me the goal is really helping the agency see the value of working with the publications who are in the citywide marketing directory.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So we have 293 publications.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've memorized the number, yes.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: All right, yes.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: In the citywide marketing directory.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And my goal is really to try and get them to spend 50% of their budget.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: with those publications.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So really that's my focus.

chapters.summary: Brewer says the FY25 report shows some large agencies, including Health and Hospitals, spent very little on advertising. Sidahmed says he will meet agencies to understand their media plans.
chapters.title: Brewer questions low ad spending by HHC and large agencies

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: About the issues like Health and Hospitals Corporation, I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They spent very little, and some of these bigger agencies, when I looked at the list, I was surprised at how little, and there were a lot of not availables on that list of agencies that are, I have the 2-5 report, I don't want to think about 2-6, but this is the 2-5 report.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There were a lot of them, some of the big ones, that spent very little money on advertising.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of why that is yet?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: No, I'm really excited to sit down with the agencies and get an understanding of their plans and how they're operating moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yes, and I can't speak to any of the media plans that were happening before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about the six firms that place city ads and whether the city needs that many. Sidahmed says their spending reports are the main source for the FY26 report and welcomes Council input on structuring the vendor system.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about six media placement vendors

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And there was also in the report, I think, about six, I call them middle men or middle agency.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: These are the groups that do the buying or, you know, is that something that you're also going to look at?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Oh, the six media placement vendors.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So as far as compiling the report, that will be the main source of information for compiling the FY26 report because all of the spend, as you mentioned, goes through them.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And then I'll need to break down each one of their spending by the different agencies because the agencies work with the...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You need that many in order to be competitive.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're always trying to save money.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I didn't know if you need six, you need four, you need three, you need different ones, or they have a contract.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How have they been decided?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: It's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'd love to collaborate with...

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: council and thinking through the future of that.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: You know, my predecessors established the system with six.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think at some point prior to that, it was just one.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And I've been hearing from different folks about the pros and cons of that system.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So if you have thoughts on that, I'd love to collaborate with council on how we structure that moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Turn it over to Councilmember Murano to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have many more.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Murano.

chapters.summary: Morano, a former broadcaster, asks whether there is inherent tension in housing MOECM under the mayor's communications office. Sidahmed says he cannot speak to prior decisions but many publishers see the office as a City Hall conduit.
chapters.title: Morano questions office independence under mayor's communications operation

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Sorry for the frog in my throat in advance.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Congratulations on your appointment, first of all.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I spend the better part of my professional life in broadcasting, so I have a tremendous appreciation for the importance of local journalism, particularly independent outlets that ask questions government officials would rather not answer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I actually agree with much of your testimony, especially your point that when local journalism disappears, government accountability.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: suffers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I want to examine whether the city is doing enough to protect the independence of the very media it's supposedly supporting.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I want to follow up on a couple of the questions the chair asked and the speaker.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In your testimony, you say your office exists in part to sustain publications that hold public officials accountable.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But in September,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The mayor moved your office under his director of communications, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Isn't there an inherent tension between supporting independent journalism and being overseen?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: By the political communications operation of the very administration those journalists are supposed to scrutinize?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Yeah, as I said, I can't really speak to the decisions that were happening prior to my arrival or how that transition happened.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: But I will say in conversations with publishers, I think many publishers see this office as a conduit to their relationship with City Hall and government.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And they do like the...

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: The placement of the office within the director of communication.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So some publishers have different opinions on it, but I think that as somebody who's almost their relationship to the government, I think that some people find it almost more natural for the office to...

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether a paper critical of Mayor Mamdani can be guaranteed no ad retaliation. Sidahmed says absolutely and supports a written prohibition on considering favorable or unfavorable coverage in ad decisions.
chapters.title: Morano seeks written ban on considering coverage in ad decisions

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, let me make it more concrete, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If a neighborhood newspaper publishes a series of highly critical articles about Mayor Mondani, can you guarantee that criticism will have absolutely no bearing on whether it receives city advertising dollars?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Would you support a written prohibition against considering favorable or unfavorable coverage when distributing city advertising?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think it's really clear to make clear that if...

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: People's coverage does not in any way influence their ability to receive or access advertising dollars.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That's why I really want to make sure that when there are questions about press or anything, I've been a journalist myself for a long time before taking this role, and I

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: would never want any journalist to feel that doing their job is going to somehow influence the bottom line of their publication.

chapters.summary: Morano cites committee findings that influencers received $5,000 to $20,000 per campaign and asks why taxpayer money goes to paid messengers while local papers struggle. Sidahmed says his focus is the 293-outlet directory.
chapters.title: Morano challenges influencer payments versus struggling neighborhood papers

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Speaking of influence, I want to follow up on what the chair mentioned, our hearing on influencers a month ago.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And this is something that troubles me as a former broadcaster.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony says we need independent journalists attending community board meetings, questioning elected officials, and investigating problems.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yet the committee report describes influencers receiving anywhere from $5,000 to $20,000 per campaign.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Some of those influencers aren't journalists at all.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're essentially paid messengers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why should taxpayer dollars be used to compensate someone for repeating government talking points when independent neighborhood newspapers are struggling to keep reporters employed?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I appreciate the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Really, my focus of my office is really my list, the citywide marketing directory list.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So the 293 publications that are in that list, those are the people that I'm really focused on trying to get as much money to as possible and working with the different agencies to see the value of working with them and using them to get their message out there.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I can't really speak to how agencies spend their money otherwise, but that's really important.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, I can tell that you're relatively new in the position because you actually answer the questions, which I really appreciate.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If taxpayer money is going to influencers, shouldn't every New Yorker know exactly who's being paid, how much they're receiving, and whether they're disclosing their relationship?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm curious, would you support public disclosure of the ultimate recipients of every dollar spent on influencer campaigns, including payments made through advertising firms and other middlemen?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: It's not really my office's responsibility to decide that or not decide that.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think my office's responsibility is really focused on getting the 50% of advertising money to community and ethnic media.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether an administration could increase social media and influencer spending, reduce traditional advertising, and still meet the 50% requirement. Sidahmed says he does not fully understand the structure but focuses on increasing dollars to community media.
chapters.title: Morano asks whether influencer spending creates a Local Law 83 loophole

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Last question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony repeatedly celebrates the city's commitment to spending 50% of advertising dollars with ethnic and community media.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But as I understand the law, that requirement only applies to certain forms of advertising.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Social media advertising and influencer campaigns fall outside of it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So theoretically, couldn't an administration dramatically increase spending on influencers, reduce traditional advertising expenditures, and still meet the 50% requirement?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So I'm not sure if I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, so it's a loophole, basically, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I mean, the requirement only applies to certain forms of advertising, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Social media advertising.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and influencer campaigns fall outside of it, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So in theory, couldn't an administration dramatically increase spending on influencers, on social media,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and reduce traditional advertising expenditures, and they're still in compliance with the law?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I can't really speak.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I fully understand the structure of that, but I think that my goal really is to increase the amount of dollars that are going out to community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That's what I'm hearing from publishers, that they need this money to survive, to keep their lights on daily.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So really that's what I'm focused on in this office, is trying to get an increased amount of dollars out the door to community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They gave me the hook, so I have more in the next round.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how outlets get on or off the 293-plus citywide marketing directory. Sidahmed says he wants to convene publishers, academics, and Council members to define community and ethnic media publicly.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how publishers are added to or removed from marketing directory

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll call on Councilmember Ressler and Wilson in a minute.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Two questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is, I think there are media individuals who would like to be on the 293-plus list.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How are you decide who is to be added or taken off of that list?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How is that conversation taking place?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I really appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: That is a concern that I've heard from many publishers.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And the concerns really vary.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think there's such a diverse number of views on...

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: What should be considered community and ethnic media?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: You know, who should be in that list?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: So what I'd like to do is actually convene a group where we have an open conversation.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: about the definition of community and ethnic media, bringing together publishers, independent academics, people who have thought about this issue extensively,

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: members of the city council who have worked with these publications for a long time and have thoughts about how we actually define what a publication who should be in a citywide marketing directory looks like.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I'd love to do that.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: I think it could be a model for the country.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: A lot of cities who have tried to execute this law have stumbled on this question.

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Who counts?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: Who should we actually put in the 50%?

utterances.speaker: Mazen Sidahmed
utterances.text: And I think we can lead by example here in New York.
